c1706.summary: Purandaradasa on the power of music: whoever plays, keeps time and sings reaches Hari.
m: He who plucked the tambura crossed the ocean of worldly life; he who kept the tala joined the gods;
he who tied on the ankle bells trampled sin; he who sang beheld the form of Hari;
he who saw Purandara Vitthala ran straight to Vaikuntha.

c5284.summary: Purandaradasa prays that the nectar of Narayana's name be on his tongue in every state of life — and above all at the final moment.
m: Narayana, may the nectar of remembering your name come to my tongue,
whether sitting or standing, singing or lying down,
so that the heaps of sins I have committed run away —
whether I go to another village or stay in my own, whatever my needs may be,
O lotus-navelled one, charioteer of Arjuna, praised by all — so that I never tire of it, time after time;
whether hungry or not, whether in delight or in joy,
O Vasudeva, destroyer of Shishupala, slayer of demons — so that I never forget your name;
whether in hardship or in prosperity, however confused my mind may be,
(the name) of the great eight-syllable mantra, as disciples say 'Krishna, Krishna';
whether dreaming or waking, whether my mind is willing or angry,
Lord of Janaka's daughter, so that I remember your lotus feet in my mind at least once;
whether fever comes or cold, whether I shiver again and again,
so that night and day I never forget to remember you as Hari Narayana, remover of sins;
always keeping your thousand names, Hari, within my heart,
O Purandara Vitthala, my king — so that I think of you at the final moment.

c1444.summary: Annamacharya: within and without, worship Govinda — Hari's names are all the mantras, and Vishnu is everything.
m: Within your thoughts and outwardly, worship saying 'Govinda, Govinda', O mind.
Hari's incarnations are all the gods; the universes are within Hari;
Hari's names are all the mantras — say 'Hari Hari Hari Hari', O mind.
Vishnu's glories are the prescribed duties; the Vedas are what praise Vishnu;
Vishnu alone is within the universe — seek 'Vishnu, Vishnu', O mind.
Achyuta alone is the beginning and the end; Achyuta is the slayer of demons;
Achyuta is on Sri Venkatadri — take refuge, saying 'Achyuta, Achyuta', O mind.

c1564.summary: Annamacharya's salutations to Narayana, the Lord of Venkata.
m: Narayana, salutations, salutations to you,
praised by Narada — salutations, salutations.
Slayer of Mura, bearer of the mountain, Mukunda, Madhava, rider of Garuda, lotus-navelled,
Supreme Person, releaser from worldly bonds — salutations; you who took the man-lion's form — salutations, salutations.
Reclining on the ocean, with sun and moon as eyes, whose feet are praised by lotus-born Brahma,
binder of Bali, beloved of the cowherd women, lotus-eyed — salutations, salutations to you.
First God, worshipped by all the Agamas, enchanting form of the Yadava clan,
rescuer of the Vedas, Lord of holy Venkata, lover of music — salutations, salutations to you.

c1040.summary: Annamacharya takes refuge at the holy feet of Sriman Narayana, the god of the Venkata hill.
m: Sriman Narayana, Sriman Narayana,
Sriman Narayana, your holy feet are my refuge.
Sun to the lotus face of Lakshmi, friend of the lotus,
dear to Lakshmi, lotus-eyed,
dear to lotus-seated Brahma, rider of Garuda, Sri
lotus-navelled one — your lotus feet are my refuge.
Fortune of the great yogis, Sri
Supreme Person, higher than the highest,
Supreme Self, subtle as the atom, Sri
God of holy Venkata hill — you are my refuge.

c1577.summary: Annamacharya points out the sacred Venkata hill: 'There it is — the abode of Hari!'
m: There it is, behold — the abode of Sri Hari,
full of the hoods of the ten thousand Sheshas.
That is Venkatachala, highest of all;
there it is, the form (worshipped by) Brahma and the others;
there it is, the eternal home of all sages —
see it, bow to it; it is full of bliss.
There nearby is Seshachala,
the true home of the gods in the sky;
there in front is the treasure stored from the beginning,
golden peaks, full of Brahman.
That Venkata mountain is the state of liberation,
the wealth of Sri Venkatapati;
to contemplate, it is the form of all riches;
it is the purest of all that purifies.

c1182.summary: Annamacharya describes the child Krishna as each of the nine gems.
m: Yashoda's darling, the pearl in her front yard,
is Devaki's son, of unequalled glory;
the ruby in the palms of the cowherd women everywhere,
the diamond against Kamsa, who held a grudge,
the emerald that lights the three worlds,
little Krishna who lives among us,
the coral of Rukmini's lips in love-play,
the hessonite of Govardhana hill,
the cat's-eye between the conch and discus,
the lotus-eyed one who is our refuge and protects us,
the topaz that pressed down on Kaliya's head,
the sapphire of Sri Venkatadri,
the divine gem never parted from the milk ocean —
Padmanabha, who looks just like a little boy.

c1602.summary: A Sanskrit song meditating on the child Gopala dancing with his bells and holding butter.
m: I meditate on the child Gopala, served by the mind; may I always contemplate his feet,
shining with the jingling of his belt of tiny bells and gem-studded ornaments,
bowing to the tinkle of his crooked steps, brilliant in his lively dance,
with butter always in his hand, whose feet shine in the contemplation of Brahma and the gods,
dwelling on holy Venkatachala, the incomparable Hari, the Supreme Person, the child Gopala.

c1000.summary: A gopi describes how her mind sways like waves at the sound of Krishna's flute.
m: My mind is swaying like waves, Kanna — swaying greatly,
at the enchanting, blissful music of your flute.
Unable to move, I stood still like a statue,
not knowing how time passed, O wondrous flute-bearer; my mind (sways).
Clear moonlight burns like broad daylight; looking toward you, my brows knit;
your ripe flute music comes on the breeze; my eyes droop, a strange feeling comes over me.
Come, steady my anxious mind, give me your feet, and rejoice; in a lonely grove embrace me and stir my feelings,
come and fulfil me — you who gave me your two feet, like the sun's rays on the waves of the ocean of art.
Shall I cry out with melting heart? Will you sport with other women? Is this fitting? Is this proper?
Is this righteous? When you play the flute, my mind aches, swaying like your earrings.

c1322.summary: Welcome, Krishna! A joyful greeting recounting Krishna's deeds.
m: Welcome, Krishna; I have come to your feet, Krishna,
dweller in Mathura, of gentle face, Madhusudana — here,
easily reached, fragrant with fine flowers and sandal,
with a musk tilaka, great one, my beloved, son of Nandagopa.
Expert wrestler who defeated Mushtika and Chanura, Madhusudana, slayer of Kuvalayapida,
who danced on Kaliya, protector of Gokula, bearing every fine mark,
protector of good people, whose resolve endures through countless aeons, unequalled,
steadfast, roaming among sages, tender as Manmatha, destroyer of demons, O God,
sweet, so sweet, daring in love, worshipped in the hearts of the young women of Vraja.

c1446.summary: The gopis complain to Yashoda about little Krishna's mischief — and one ends by describing how he showed her all of Vaikuntha.
m: Mother Yashoda, hear of the tricks played by the magician born in your cowherd clan,
Gopalakrishna — listen!
Listen, woman — a child like your son, in this
world, ammamma, I have never seen.
With anklets jingling on his feet, bangles tinkling on his hands, pearl garlands swaying, he came to our door,
swinging feet and hands in time to the tala, the blue-hued Kanna danced.
Thinking him a little boy I leapt and hugged him; as I hugged him, like a bridegroom he kissed me on the mouth, girl.
He's no child, your son — Krishna who plays so many tricks; I'm too ashamed to say it for others to hear.
The other day, a guest who came this way lay tired and asleep — Kannan
ate the butter, and the butter left in his hand he smeared in the guest's mouth and hid —
the blame fell here, the sin there; is it fitting to cause such grief?
What great penance did Nandagopa do to get such a child? What shall we do, girl?
He begged 'butter, butter'; when I gave him butter he ate it up, then winked and asked for a girl.
Dancing gracefully, he kicked up dust with his feet, threw it in my eyes, and stole.
He played the flute so tunefully; as I stood listening, he came near and teased me.
All the merits of womankind, crores upon crores, seem to be yours, girl — and it is all slipping away from us.
The other evening he came close, as if he were kin, and played many tricks;
saying 'I'll let go only if you give me a ball of butter', he pulled my saree end and fought.
This is that Vasudeva himself, Yashoda; thinking him a child I pulled him onto my lap —
and as my mind swooned at his beautiful face, he showed me everything, Vaikuntha and all.
He pinched the baby in the cradle, and as it wailed
he ate the butter while the mother left her work.
He untied the tethered calf and, kicking, hid it,
and tied the rope around his own neck instead.
Then he cried 'Amma!' like the calf,
and the cow without her calf answered 'Amma!'
With a lily in his hand, your precious son reached up
and drinks the milk straight from the cow in the shed, girl!
Circling around me, he asked the way to his aunt's house;
I stood telling him until he understood;
was he satisfied? He asked the way to the riverbank;
I stood telling him all that too;
cleverly he asked one more thing — I'm ashamed!
He asked the way to a kiss, and made a fuss, girl!
You've given him so much freedom and raised him so softly;
it's no fault to tell you all this about him, girl!

c1219.summary: A gopi says that even after Krishna stole her heart with his flute, she has no complaint — and describes him dancing in the moonlight.
m: Even after he played the flute and stole my whole heart, what complaint can I have, friend?
As the lovely peacock dances,
and like a creeper swaying in the breeze,
in the shining moonlight that delights the heart, flocks of birds call, forgetting themselves,
my heart longing to see the beauty of him swaying and running joyfully,
singing a verse — 'this is fitting' — and dancing to 'takita tadhimi',
with calves and cows standing around him, the Lord whose face blooms with love,
his makara earrings swaying and his crown shining to match,
most beautiful, his garment fluttering in the breeze.

c8618.summary: Wherever the devotee looks — the sky, a pond, a cuckoo's song — Krishna's face and flute appear.
m: Thinking of your innocent face, dripping with milk, my heart is overwhelmed, Kanna.
Beautiful one, dark as the blue sea, who made my heart his home,
from that day until today, whatever I see, my thoughts never leave you.
Even if my mind looks up to the sky, your enchanting form appears; clearly,
even if my thoughts turn to a clear pond, your smiling face appears; a little,
even if I listen to the cuckoo's song, the sound of your flute bewilders me there.
With your dark curls and a peacock feather tucked in, on the riverbank,
with the peacocks and the hushed cuckoos singing, by the blue river and in the sky,
in your young hand that shines with the flute, the music that makes voice, beauty and movement melt,
in the play of your two lotus eyes, like the sun and moon,
on Kaliya's head, on your stamping foot — fixing my mind there,
in dream and waking, birth after birth, melting in love — come near and grant your supreme compassion.

c1298.summary: Vyasaraja calls on the child Krishna of Udupi to come quickly, describing his ornaments.
m: Krishna, come quickly.
Come quickly, show me your face.
Anklet bells on your feet, a blue bracelet,
come dancing, blue-hued one.
Little bells at your waist, rings on your fingers,
the Vaijayanti garland around your neck,
yellow Kashi silk, a flute in your hand,
fragrant sandal paste smeared on your body!
You who showed the whole world in your mouth to your mother,
uplifter of the world, our Sri Krishna of Udupi.

c2975.summary: Sadasiva Brahmendra urges the tongue to drink the nectar of Rama's name.
m: Drink the nectar of Rama, O tongue; drink the nectar of Rama.
It drives away all contact with sin; it is full of every kind of reward;
it removes the fear and sorrow of birth and death; it is the essence of all Shastras, Vedas and Agamas;
it protected the cosmic egg born of the lotus; it made even heretics supremely pure;
it is sung in the pure order of the Paramahamsas; it was drunk by Shuka, Shaunaka, Kaushika and others.

c1059.summary: Sadasiva Brahmendra asks the mind to roam in Brahman — that is, in Krishna.
m: Roam, O mind, in Brahman; roam, O mind —
(in him) whose hair is adorned with the feathers of the proud peacock, whose glorious cheeks outshine mirrors,
who sports in Lakshmi's embrace, the wish-tree in the homes of those who serve,
the moon to the chakora birds that are the great ascetics, who fills (the world) with the sound of the flute.

c1054.summary: Worship Gopala, O mind — the friend of Kuchela, root of the three worlds.
m: Worship Gopala, O mind; worship Gopala.
Worship Gopala, worshipped by Kuchela, root of the three worlds, death to the sons of Diti,
essence of the Agamas, the object of yogic contemplation, of beautiful body, support of the worlds,
fierce in battle, far from impurity, lovely as Madana, slayer of Madhu,
wish-tree to those who bow, son of Nanda, slayer of Chanura, the swan who roams (in pure hearts).

c2971.summary: Rama plays in my heart — the heart is Ayodhya, and peace is his Sita.
m: Rama plays in my heart; he plays in my heart —
the ferry across the great ocean of delusion, slayer of the demons of desire, hatred and the rest,
companion of peace, the daughter of Videha, who roams in Ayodhya, the cave of the heart,
who upholds the empire of the Paramahamsa, whose body is truth, knowledge and bliss.

c1364.summary: Say 'Mukunda', O tongue — a litany of Krishna's names.
m: Say 'Mukunda', O tongue; say 'Mukunda'.
Say 'Keshava, Madhava, Govinda', 'Krishna, bliss, eternal bliss';
say 'Radha's beloved, Hari, Rama', 'lotus-eyed, cloud-dark one';
say 'rider of Garuda, holder of the Nandaka sword', 'who cut off the ten-headed one's heads';
say 'dear to Akrura, bearer of the discus', 'the swan, the stainless one, slayer of Kamsa'.

c2511.summary: All is Brahman — so what is there to say or not say, to do or not do?
m: All is Brahman, O!
What is to be said, what is not to be said? What is to be made, what is not to be made?
What is to be read, what is not to be read? What is to be worshipped, what is not to be worshipped?
What is to be known, what is not to be known? What is to be enjoyed, what is not to be enjoyed?
Everywhere and always, practise meditation on the Self (Hamsa) — it is the source of liberation.

c2440.summary: Muttu Tandavar's vivid description of Nataraja dancing in the golden hall of Chidambaram — would two eyes be enough to see it?
m: He danced! To see that spectacle, shouldn't one have a thousand eyes?
He who dwells beside those who seek and praise him, our Lord of the holy golden hall —
as the anklets on his lotus feet swayed and the bells on his feet rang 'kin kin',
as the tiger skin he flayed and wore swayed proudly,
as the deer and axe in his red hands swayed, as the dwarf Muyalagan and his red-gold earrings swayed,
as the Ganga and the young crescent in his red matted hair swayed, in the golden hall —
as garlands of nine gems swayed, as the dancing serpent spread its hood and swayed,
as the lovely garland of konrai flowers swayed, as the people of Chidambaram danced,
as the three thousand great Vedic Brahmins of Tillai worshipped and danced,
as dark Kali danced facing him, in the golden hall —
as dancing Ganapati and Velan (Murugan) danced, as Brahma with Vishnu and Indra danced,
as the thirty-three crore gods danced, and the sages too,
as Patanjali of true devotion danced, and Vyaghrapada and Nandi danced,
as Sivakami Amma, with her lovely ears, danced along with him.

c1035.summary: Gopalakrishna Bharati: is any god equal to Sabhapati (Nataraja) of Chidambaram? Saying 'Shiva Chidambaram' once is enough.
m: Is any other god equal to Sabhapati of Tillai?
Can one find on this earth a treasure of compassion like him?
If one says even once 'Shiva Chidambaram', it is enough;
need one perform any other merit for liberation?
The Purana tells how the three great saint-poets attained his feet;
we have heard it told — so sings Gopalakrishna of Tillai.

c1250.summary: From Nandanar Charitram: the outcaste devotee Nandanar asks Nataraja whether he may come near to see his dance.
m: May I come, sir, near you, to stand and celebrate you and sing?
Aren't you the supreme treasure of compassion? Should this outcaste need to speak words of courtesy?
There, to see your supremely blissful dance, I —
born an outcaste on this earth, I lived without doing any merit;
Lord, I have come to your presence; I have lost the ocean of births; the shore
I have reached, I have taken refuge; O giver of boons of Tillai, remove my suffering and sins.

c1487.summary: Nilakanta Sivan's description of Nataraja dancing the dance of bliss in Chidambaram.
m: He dances the dance of bliss in the hall of Tillai —
for those who bow at his feet there is no defeat.
As faithful devotees join their palms, as gods and sages praise him, as the restless-eyed
Uma watches in delight — 'takita tarikita tongita dhittimi dhimi taka tatingina takatom' —
pressing one foot on fortunate Muyalagan, lifting the other foot as devotees worship,
making the creators and protectors his drummers — Lord of space, Chidambara Shambhu, Sadashiva, the beautiful one —
as the gem-bells at his waist jingle and the serpent ornaments clink,
as the crescent moon's light flashes and his anklets ring 'ghalir ghalir',
as the blue throat that swallowed the poison shines — destroyer of the cities, beautiful Shiva, gracious supreme guru, Shiva Shankara —
as the cosmos and the body dance, as the eight directions sing his praise.

c1305.summary: Who but Rama will protect me? I cannot let go of his lotus feet.
m: Who is there to protect me other than you, Raghuvara? I cannot leave your lotus feet, abode of compassion.
O you worshipped by four-faced Brahma and others, why this indifference? Your deeds
I have not tired of praising; end my worries, grant me boons, and quickly (protect) me.
Lord of Sita, have you no affection for me? You whose feet Hanuman worships, won't you hear my cries?
Aren't you the Vasudeva who rushed to save the elephant king? Drive away all my sins, hold my hand firmly, and never let me go.

c4025.summary: A brisk hymn to Rama, moon to the ocean of the Raghu race, identified with Venkateshvara.
m: Moon to the ocean of nectar of the Raghu race, Sri Rama, king of kings,
wind to the clouds of sin, giver of good, lion to the demon kings, noble lord of the world,
who crushed the pride of Parashurama, victorious one, at whose battles Rudra and others marvelled,
ornament of the Solar race, of countless wondrous valour, Sri Venkatesha,
who humbled Bhrigu's son and broke the monkey king's pride, friend of the hosts of gods,
protector of the wise who know the Vedanta, lotus-eyed Sri Venkateshvara,
who crushed the pride of Parashurama, victorious one, at whose battles Rudra and others marvelled,
ornament of the Solar race, of countless wondrous valour, Sri Venkateshvara.

c1045.summary: A hymn to the Goddess, full of nectar, who holds the sugarcane bow — in Amritavarshini, the raga said to bring rain.
m: Full of nectar, treasury of nectar, holder of the sugarcane bow with flower arrows,
praised by Brahma and Indra, pure one, (protect me) always, essence of the Vedas, Vijayambika,
lotus-eyed, enchantress of the world, adorned with gems of melodious ragas, beloved of Harikesha, who draws out the nectar of bliss.

c1068.summary: A Kannada song: remember Bhuvaneshvari, O mind — she frees one from the fear of worldly bonds.
m: Remember Bhuvaneshvari, O mind; she frees you from the fear of worldly bonds.
With her, in this world, one is never empty, never weary, never in pain; she cools and comforts with grace.
(Remember) the mother who destroys sins, Mother of the three worlds, beyond the three gunas,
the noble divine cow who protects her own devotees, praised by Brahma, beloved of Sri Harikesha.

c3245.summary: A varnam: the heroine longs for Lord Srinivasa and asks him to protect her.
m: I have longed for you, Lord of all the worlds.
This is the time to protect me; look on me with grace,
O one of praised form, Srinivasa.

c3452.summary: A varnam: on whose advice is Venkatesha acting so coldly? The heroine cannot bear Manmatha's arrows.
m: On whose advice do you act like this?
Take me as yours quickly, Sri Venkatesha, lord of the Seshachala hills.
I cannot bear the arrows of Manmatha.

c1821.summary: A varnam: the heroine, infatuated with Lord Kumara (Murugan), asks him to come to her.
m: Lord, longing for you, I have become greatly infatuated.
Without delay, look on me with compassion, Kumara.
This lotus-eyed one, on you —
this lotus-eyed one has fallen in love with you; come to her tonight for love's play, and honour her, Kumara.
